claims.source: Here, we show that late endosomes of VE cells exhibit different modes of fusion with target organelles depending on their targets: they undergo homotypic fusion with late endosomes in an explosive fusion-like manner and heterotypic fusion with lysosomes in a bridge fusion-like manner.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and introduction, supported by experimental observations described in the Results section

claims.claim: Vesicle size is a critical determinant of fusion types.
claims.source: Mathematical modeling showed that vesicle size is a critical determinant of these fusion types and that membrane fluctuation forces can overcome the vesicle size effects.
claims.evidence: Supported by mathematical modeling results presented in the manuscript

claims.claim: Membrane fluctuation forces can overcome vesicle size effects on fusion type.
claims.source: Mathematical modeling showed that vesicle size is a critical determinant of these fusion types and that membrane fluctuation forces can overcome the vesicle size effects.
claims.evidence: Supported by mathematical modeling results and experimental data with actin inhibitors

claims.claim: Actin filaments are bound to late endosomes in VE cells.
claims.source: We found that actin filaments were bound to late endosomes and forces derived from dynamic actin remodeling were necessary for quick fusion during homotypic fusion.
claims.evidence: Supported by phalloidin staining and microscopy data shown in Figure 5

claims.claim: Forces derived from dynamic actin remodeling are necessary for quick fusion during homotypic fusion.
claims.source: We found that actin filaments were bound to late endosomes and forces derived from dynamic actin remodeling were necessary for quick fusion during homotypic fusion.
claims.evidence: Supported by experiments with cytochalasin D and jasplakinolide showing altered fusion dynamics

claims.claim: Cofilin plays a role in endocytic fusion by regulating actin turnover.
claims.source: Furthermore, cofilin played a role in endocytic fusion by regulating actin turnover.
claims.evidence: Supported by experiments with S3 peptide (cofilin activator) showing effects on fusion frequency and actin dynamics

claims.claim: Actin promotes vesicle fusion for efficient membrane trafficking in visceral endoderm cells.
claims.source: These data suggest that actin promotes vesicle fusion for efficient membrane trafficking in visceral endoderm cells.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results showing actin's role in fusion

claims.claim: Different types of endosomal vesicles are aligned from the apical to the basal area in the supranuclear portion of VE cells.
claims.source: These observations revealed that different types of endosomal vesicles were aligned from the apical to the basal area in the supranuclear portion of VE cells, reflecting the repeated fusion and enlargement of vesicles as they migrated deeper into the cell (Figure 1B and C).
claims.evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy observations and organelle marker staining shown in Figure 1

claims.claim: Small vesicles in zone 1 (within 0.5-1 μm of the apical surface) are positive for EEA1, indicating they are early endosomes.
claims.source: In the most superficial portion (within 0.5–1 μm of the apical surface; designated as zone 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), fuzzy FM1-43 staining was observed (Figure 1B). The small vesicles in this zone were positive for EEA1 (Figure 1B), indicating that they were early endosomes.
claims.evidence: Supported by immunostaining data with EEA1 antibody shown in Figure 1B

claims.claim: Medium-sized round vesicles in zone 2 (at a depth of 1-6 μm from the apical surface) are positive for Rab7, suggesting they are late endosomes.
claims.source: Immediately beneath zone 1, many medium-sized round vesicles were observed (zone 2; at a depth of 1–6 μm from the apical surface, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A). Electroporation of EGFP-Rab7 revealed that these vesicles were positive for Rab7, suggesting that they were late endosomes.
claims.evidence: Supported by EGFP-Rab7 expression data shown in Figure 1B

claims.claim: Large amorphous lysosomes in zone 3 (at a depth of 6-16 μm from the apical surface) are positive for LysoTracker Red and LAMP1.
claims.source: In the deep portion (zone 3; at a depth of 6–16 μm from the apical surface, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), large amorphous lysosomes, positive for LysoTracker Red and LAMP1, were observed (Figure 1B; Koike et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Supported by LysoTracker Red staining and LAMP1 immunostaining shown in Figure 1B

claims.claim: Endocytosed transferrin is rapidly transported from early endosomes to lysosomes via late endosomes in VE cells.
claims.source: The time course of the numbers of labeled vesicles in each zone showed that endocytosed transferrin was rapidly transported from early endosomes to lysosomes via late endosomes in VE cells, as reported previously (Richardson et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging of Alexa 488-transferrin shown in Figure 1D and E

claims.claim: In homotypic fusion, two late endosomes fuse quickly in an explosive mode where a membrane pore quickly expands.
claims.source: First, from 5 min after pulse labeling, fusion of two neighboring late endosomes was observed frequently (Figure 2A and B; Video 1). The fusion showed an explosive mode, in which a membrane pore quickly expanded and two vesicles fused to become a single vesicle (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2 and Video 1

claims.claim: Homotypic fusion is completed within 20-50 seconds (mean 31.9±0.2 s, n=37).
claims.source: The fusion was completed within 20–50 s (the time required from membrane fusion to single spherical vesicle formation was 31.9±0.2 s, n=37), and the time was weakly correlated with the vesicle size (r=0.60, Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2D

claims.claim: The time required for homotypic fusion completion is weakly correlated with vesicle size (r=0.60).
claims.source: The fusion was completed within 20–50 s (the time required from membrane fusion to single spherical vesicle formation was 31.9±0.2 s, n=37), and the time was weakly correlated with the vesicle size (r=0.60, Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2D

claims.claim: Late endosomes of any size undergo homotypic fusion.
claims.source: The size distribution of the late endosomes that underwent fusion (7.3±6.6 μm2, n=34) was similar to that of the total late endosomes in the observed area at the start of recording (5.7±6.4 μm2, n=265; Figure 2C), indicating that late endosomes of any size underwent homotypic fusion.
claims.evidence: Supported by size distribution analysis shown in Figure 2C

claims.claim: Heterotypic fusion between late endosomes and lysosomes occurs as bridge fusion where the pore does not expand and the late endosome gradually shrinks.
claims.source: Second, from 15 min after pulse labeling, some late endosomes shrank gradually and disappeared from the focal plane (Figure 3A and Video 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 3 and Video 2

claims.claim: The disappearance of late endosomes is a consequence of fusion with underlying lysosomes, not engulfment, in E8.5 embryos.
claims.source: These data suggest that the disappearance of late endosomes is a consequence of fusion with the underlying lysosomes, but not of engulfment in E8.5 embryos.
claims.evidence: Supported by differential labeling experiments and electron microscopy showing pore formation between late endosomes and lysosomes

claims.claim: Heterotypic fusion is slower than homotypic fusion and is completed within 90-250 seconds (mean 154.8±1.4 s, n=25).
claims.source: This type of fusion, so-called bridge fusion, described in a previous study (Nicot et al., 2006; Roberts et al., 1999), occurred as a result of the slow mixing of vesicular contents through a narrow fusion pore. Actually, heterotypic fusion was slower than homotypic fusion and was completed within 90–250 s (154.8±1.4 s, n=25), and the fusion time (the time required from membrane fusion to disappearance of the vesicle) did not correlate with the vesicle size (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 3F

claims.claim: The fusion time in heterotypic fusion does not correlate with vesicle size.
claims.source: Actually, heterotypic fusion was slower than homotypic fusion and was completed within 90–250 s (154.8±1.4 s, n=25), and the fusion time (the time required from membrane fusion to disappearance of the vesicle) did not correlate with the vesicle size (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3F

claims.claim: Larger late endosomes tend to undergo heterotypic fusion.
claims.source: The size of the labeled late endosomes at this time point (10.1±8.1 μm2, n=256) was larger than that at 5 min after labeling (6.7±6.2 μm2, n=242), indicating that larger late endosomes tended to undergo heterotypic fusion (Figure 3G, see also below).
claims.evidence: Supported by size distribution analysis at different time points shown in Figure 3G

claims.claim: The size of late endosomes is not the sole trigger for heterotypic fusion.
claims.source: However, the size of the late endosomes that underwent heterotypic fusion (10.2±9.2 μm2, n=34) did not differ from that of the total late endosomes at 15 min after labeling (Figure 3G), indicating that the size of late endosomes is not the sole trigger for heterotypic fusion.
claims.evidence: Supported by size distribution comparison shown in Figure 3G

claims.claim: The free energy of a vesicle consists of bending energy and osmotic energy.
claims.source: According to thermodynamics, the deformation of a physical object proceeds as its free energy decreases. The free energy of a vesicle consists of two terms: bending energy and osmotic energy.
claims.evidence: This is based on established thermodynamic principles applied to vesicle systems

claims.claim: Vesicle size intrinsically affects the balance of bending energy and osmotic energy and may be a critical factor for membrane deformation during fusion.
claims.source: Note that the bending energy depends only on its shape; in other words, two membranes with the same shape but with different sizes have the same bending energy. On the other hand, the volume depends on both the size and the shape. Therefore, the vesicle size intrinsically affects the balance of both energy sources and may be a critical factor for membrane deformation during fusion.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical inference from the mathematical model

claims.claim: Mathematical modeling predicts that late endosomes are large enough to allow bridge fusion to occur, although they exhibit explosive fusion in vivo.
claims.source: Our modeling predicted that the late endosomes are large enough to allow bridge fusion to occur, although they exhibit explosive fusion in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction from the mathematical model that contrasts with experimental observations

claims.claim: Membrane fluctuation is a critical factor determining fusion mode beyond vesicle size.
claims.source: These observations indicate that vesicle size is not the sole factor determining the fusion mode. Lipid composition, a well-known parameter affecting its bending modulus, is also involved, but the effect on fusion mode may be less dominant when compared with the vesicle size effects (Simson et al., 1998; Faizi et al., 2019; Ridolfi et al., 2021). One of the critical factors other than vesicle size that determine the fusion mode is membrane fluctuation.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the discrepancy between model predictions and experimental observations, supported by citations

claims.claim: Homotypic fusion is converted to bridge-like fusion after cytochalasin D treatment.
claims.source: We found that homotypic fusion was converted to bridge-like fusion after cytochalasin D treatment (Figure 7C), which suggests that actin dynamics around vesicles cause fluctuation and affect the fusion modes.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data with cytochalasin D shown in Figure 7C

claims.claim: Actin dynamics around vesicles cause fluctuation and affect fusion modes.
claims.source: We found that homotypic fusion was converted to bridge-like fusion after cytochalasin D treatment (Figure 7C), which suggests that actin dynamics around vesicles cause fluctuation and affect the fusion modes.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the cytochalasin D experimental results

claims.claim: A larger fluctuation can shift the fusion mode from bridge to explosive fusion.
claims.source: This finding can be successfully explained by introducing minor modifications in our mathematical modeling so that a larger fluctuation can shift the fusion mode from bridge to explosive fusion.
claims.evidence: Supported by Monte Carlo simulations shown in Figure 4F

claims.claim: VE cells vigorously endocytose maternal proteins and supply digested products to the developing embryo to support embryonic development.
claims.source: VE cells vigorously endocytose maternal proteins and supply the digested products to the developing embryo to support embryonic development.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about VE cell function

claims.claim: Larger vesicle size leads to reduction in vesicle fusion speed and subsequent nutrient trafficking efficiency.
claims.source: However, larger vesicle size leads to the reduction in the vesicle fusion speed and subsequent nutrient trafficking efficiency.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference from the relationship between vesicle size and fusion dynamics

claims.claim: Forces generated by actin increase the rate of vesicular trafficking and overcome the disadvantage of large vesicle size.
claims.source: If vesicle size were the only factor determining the fusion mode, this disadvantage would occur, but if fluctuation is taken into account, it can be overcome, as shown in our mathematical modeling, and the forces generated by actin are thought to be responsible for increasing the rate of vesicular trafficking.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the mathematical modeling and experimental results

claims.claim: Knockout mice of actin-related genes (Arc and Myh9) show abnormal VE cells and embryonic lethality.
claims.source: This idea is supported by previous reports that knockout mice of actin-related genes (e.g. Arc and Myh9) showed abnormal VE cells and embryonic lethality (Conti et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claims.claim: In heterotypic fusion, lysosomes are too large compared to late endosomes and actin accumulation on lysosomal membrane is scarce, resulting in insufficient force for explosive fusion.
claims.source: In heterotypic fusion, late endosomes fused with lysosomes in a bridge-like manner. This may be because lysosomes are too large in comparison with late endosomes and actin accumulation on the lysosomal membrane is scarce, resulting in insufficient force of actin for explosive fusion.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed heterotypic fusion mode

claims.claim: Two types of actin filaments are associated with late endosomes in VE cells: those extending along the apical-basal axis and those extending radially from the endosomes.
claims.source: We found two types of actin filaments associated with late endosomes in VE cells: those that extended along the apical-basal axis and those that extended radially from the endosomes (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: Supported by high-resolution imaging data shown in Figure 5

claims.claim: Strong actin signals are detected associated with the cell membrane in VE cells.
claims.source: In VE cells, strong signals were detected to be associated with the cell membrane (Figure 5A–C).
claims.evidence: Supported by phalloidin staining shown in Figure 5A-C

claims.claim: Small punctates and short filaments of actin are detected in the cytoplasm in zone 2 and are bound to the surface of late endosomes.
claims.source: In zone 2, small punctates and short filaments were detected in the cytoplasm (Figure 5B) and were bound to the surface of late endosomes (Figure 5B, B' and B'') and infrequently to lysosomes in zone 3 (Figure 5C, C' and C'').
claims.evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 5B and 5C

claims.claim: Several rod-like actin filaments extend from the apical side of VE cells into the cytoplasm and surround and hold late endosomes.
claims.source: Optical cross-sectional images and 3D reconstruction showed that several rod-like actin filaments, extending from the apical side of VE cells into the cytoplasm, surrounded and held the late endosomes (Figure 5D–F).
claims.evidence: Supported by 3D reconstruction images shown in Figure 5D-F

claims.claim: Most actin punctates observed in the x-y plane correspond to cross-sectional images of actin filaments extending in the apical-to-basal direction.
claims.source: These data indicate that most actin punctates observed in the x-y plane correspond to the cross-sectional images of actin filaments extending in the apical-to-basal direction.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the 3D reconstruction data

claims.claim: Most actin punctates surrounding late endosomes are bundled.
claims.source: In addition, when a fusion protein of an actin-bundling protein, fascin-1, with a red fluorescent protein was expressed in VE cells by electroporation, fascin-1 was highly colocalized with the actin punctates, suggesting that most of the actin punctates surrounding the late endosomes were bundled (Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: Supported by fascin-1 colocalization data shown in Figure 5G

claims.claim: Fine actin filaments extend radially from endosomal membranes in the x-y plane.
claims.source: To investigate the endosome-associated actin filaments in more detail, we performed high-resolution imaging analysis using a deconvolution technique, which had resolution comparable to super-resolution microscopy. It demonstrated that fine actin filaments extended radially from the endosomal membranes in the x-y plane, in addition to the actin filaments extending in the apical-basal axis (Figure 5H).
claims.evidence: Supported by deconvolution microscopy images shown in Figure 5H

claims.claim: Actin turnover on the surface of late endosomes is dynamically regulated, with a tendency to be more active in the apical area than in the basal area.
claims.source: These results indicated that actin turnover on the surface of late endosomes was dynamically regulated, with a tendency to be more active in the apical area than in the basal area.
claims.evidence: Supported by FRAP assay data showing different recovery times in apical vs basal regions (Figure 6C-E)

claims.claim: When late endosomes move in the x-y plane in zone 2, spots of EGFP-actin are always at the rear-end of the endosomes along the moving direction.
claims.source: The time-lapse images showed that when late endosomes moved in an x-y plane in zone 2, spots of EGFP-actin were always at the rear-end of the endosomes along the moving direction (Figure 6F, n=13).
claims.evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 6F

claims.claim: Arp2/3-dependent actin polymerization on the membrane acts as the driving force of motility of intracellular pathogens and endosomes/lysosomes in Xenopus egg extracts.
claims.source: Because it is known that Arp2/3-dependent actin polymerization on the membrane acts as the driving force of the motility of intracellular pathogens (Welch and Way, 2013) and endosomes/lysosomes in Xenopus egg extracts (Taunton et al., 2000), we examined the localization of Arp2/3 in VE cells to test the possible role of Arp2/3 in endosome migration.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claims.claim: Arp3-EGFP signals are distributed in dots on late endosomes and partially colocalize with phalloidin spots in the x-y plane in zone 2.
claims.source: When a fusion protein of Arp3-EGFP was expressed in VE cells by electroporation, the EGFP signals were distributed in dots on the late endosomes and partially colocalized with phalloidin spots in the x-y plane in zone 2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: Supported by Arp3-EGFP localization data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B

claims.claim: Arp3-EGFP signals are always seen at the rear-end of endosomes along the moving direction.
claims.source: In addition, Arp3-EGFP signals were always seen at the rear-end of the endosomes along the moving direction (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C

claims.claim: Radial branched filaments are temporally polymerized to provide propulsive force on the membrane for intracellular movement.
claims.source: Taken together, these data suggest that the radial branched filaments are temporally polymerized to provide the propulsive force on the membrane for intracellular movement.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the Arp3 localization and actin dynamics data

claims.claim: Treatment with cytochalasin D reduces the frequency of homotypic fusion in a dose-dependent manner.
claims.source: Treatment with cytochalasin D (a cell-permeable inhibitor of actin polymerization) for 5 min significantly changed the distribution of actin filaments. High-resolution imaging analysis using a deconvolution technique showed that phalloidin-positive filamentous structures decreased and instead actin aggregation was observed in the cytosol (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A). The treatment reduced the frequency of homotypic fusion in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 7A and B; Video 3).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data with cytochalasin D shown in Figure 7A and B

claims.claim: Treatment with 0.1 or 1.0 μM cytochalasin D slows down homotypic fusion.
claims.source: In addition, it altered the speed and mode of the fusion. Treatment with 0.1 or 1.0 μM cytochalasin D slowed down homotypic fusion (Figure 7C and D; Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 7C and D

claims.claim: Upon 1.0 μM cytochalasin D treatment, about one-third of homotypic fusion shows bridge fusion.
claims.source: Furthermore, upon 1.0 μM cytochalasin D treatment, about one-third of homotypic fusion showed bridge fusion (Figure 7C and E; Video 4).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 7C and E

claims.claim: Cytochalasin D slows down fusion processes and changes the fusion mode to bridge fusion at higher concentrations.
claims.source: Therefore, cytochalasin D slowed down the fusion processes and changed the fusion mode to bridge fusion at higher concentrations.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the cytochalasin D experimental results

claims.claim: Treatment with jasplakinolide reduces the frequency of homotypic fusion in a dose-dependent manner.
claims.source: Treatment with jasplakinolide (a cell-permeable stabilizer of actin filaments) also changed the actin dynamics. After the treatment, the actin meshwork beneath the plasma membrane (zone 1) was denser (Figure 7—figure supplement 2). Furthermore, actin filaments extending radially from the late endosomes were thicker and the fluorescence intensity was increased, although the actin filaments extending from the apical-basal axis were not changed (Figure 7—figure supplement 2). The treatment reduced the frequency of homotypic fusion in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 7A and B; Video 5), indicating that dynamic actin turnover is required for homotypic fusion.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data with jasplakinolide shown in Figure 7A and B

claims.claim: Dynamic actin turnover is required for homotypic fusion.
claims.source: The treatment reduced the frequency of homotypic fusion in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 7A and B; Video 5), indicating that dynamic actin turnover is required for homotypic fusion.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the jasplakinolide experimental results

claims.claim: When late endosomes undergo fusion, EGFP-actin punctates are excluded from membrane docking sites and highly polymerized transiently at both ends of fusing vesicles during the rounding period.
claims.source: We next observed the distribution of actin filaments during homotypic fusion. When late endosomes underwent fusion, EGFP-actin punctates were excluded from the membrane docking sites and highly polymerized transiently at both ends of the fusing vesicles (opposite to the docking region) during the rounding period after membrane fusion (Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging of EGFP-actin during fusion shown in Figure 7F

claims.claim: Actin filament distribution is spatially regulated during fusion.
claims.source: The fluorescence intensity of EGFP-actin on endosomes was quantitated in the proximal, lateral, and distal regions at the predocking, docking, rounding, and postfusion stages. This analysis indicated that actin filament distribution was spatially regulated during fusion (Figure 7G, dark gray bar), whereas FM 1–43 distribution, used as an unchanged control, was uniform on the membrane throughout the rounding stages (Figure 7G, light gray bar).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of EGFP-actin distribution shown in Figure 7G

claims.claim: The total fluorescence intensity of EGFP-actin on late endosomes significantly increases transiently after pore formation.
claims.source: Furthermore, the total fluorescence intensity of EGFP-actin on late endosomes significantly increased transiently after pore formation (Figure 7H), indicating that actin filaments were polymerized temporarily, not simply distributed differently.
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 7H

claims.claim: Actin filaments are polymerized temporarily during fusion, not simply distributed differently.
claims.source: Furthermore, the total fluorescence intensity of EGFP-actin on late endosomes significantly increased transiently after pore formation (Figure 7H), indicating that actin filaments were polymerized temporarily, not simply distributed differently.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the increase in total EGFP-actin fluorescence intensity

claims.claim: Treatment with CK-666 (an Arp2/3 inhibitor) results in a decrease in the frequency of homotypic fusion and slows down homotypic fusion.
claims.source: Moreover, accumulation of Arp3-EGFP in the distal region during the rounding stage was observed similarly to EGFP-actin accumulation (Figure 7—figure supplement 4), and treatment with CK-666, an Arp2/3 inhibitor, resulted in a decrease in the frequency of homotypic fusion (Figure 7B) and slowed down homotypic fusion (Figure 7C and D).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data with CK-666 shown in Figure 7B, C, and D

claims.claim: Branched actin filaments nucleated by the Arp2/3 complex on the distal surface of late endosomes are necessary to transform the vesicle into a large round sphere quickly after membrane fusion.
claims.source: These results suggest that branched actin filaments nucleated by the Arp2/3 complex on the distal surface of late endosomes are necessary to transform the vesicle into a large round sphere quickly after membrane fusion of late endosomes.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the Arp3 localization and CK-666 inhibition data

claims.claim: Cytochalasin D treatment leads to a significant reduction in the frequency of heterotypic fusion in a dose-dependent manner.
claims.source: We next examined the role of actin filaments in heterotypic fusion. Cytochalasin D treatment led to a significant reduction in the frequency of heterotypic fusion in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 8A–C and Video 6).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data with cytochalasin D shown in Figure 8A-C

claims.claim: Jasplakinolide treatment does not inhibit heterotypic fusion and increases the frequency of heterotypic fusion with lysosomes at 5 min after pulse labeling.
claims.source: In contrast, jasplakinolide treatment did not inhibit heterotypic fusion and somehow increased the frequency of heterotypic fusion with lysosomes at as early as 5 min after pulse labeling (Figure 8B and Video 7).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data with jasplakinolide shown in Figure 8B

claims.claim: CK-666 treatment has no effects on heterotypic fusion, suggesting that Arp2/3 is not required for heterotypic fusion.
claims.source: In addition, CK-666 treatment had no effects, suggesting that Arp2/3 was not required for heterotypic fusion (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data with CK-666 shown in Figure 8C

claims.claim: Actin plays distinct roles in homotypic fusion and heterotypic fusion.
claims.source: These data suggest that actin played distinct roles in homotypic fusion and heterotypic fusion and that stable actin filaments are implicated in driving heterotypic fusion.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of actin inhibitors on the two fusion types

claims.claim: Stable actin filaments are implicated in driving heterotypic fusion.
claims.source: These data suggest that actin played distinct roles in homotypic fusion and heterotypic fusion and that stable actin filaments are implicated in driving heterotypic fusion.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the jasplakinolide results showing increased heterotypic fusion

claims.claim: Heterotypic fusion frequency is reduced to 20% by MyoVin-1 (myosin V inhibitor) and to a lesser extent by blebbistatin (NM II inhibitor).
claims.source: Heterotypic fusion frequency was reduced to 20% by MyoVin-1 and to a lesser extent, but significantly, by blebbistatin, but was not affected by PClP or TIP (Figure 8D).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data with myosin inhibitors shown in Figure 8D

claims.claim: Homotypic fusion frequency is significantly reduced by PClP (myosin I inhibitor), MyoVin-1 (myosin V inhibitor), and TIP (myosin VI inhibitor).
claims.source: In contrast, homotypic fusion frequency was significantly reduced by PClP, MyoVin-1, and TIP (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data with myosin inhibitors shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1

claims.claim: EGFP-myosin IIA signals overlap with phalloidin-positive spots on late endosomes.
claims.source: EGFP-myosin IIA signals overlapped with phalloidin-positive spots on late endosomes (Figure 8E), whereas EGFP-myosin Va signals were juxtaposed to phalloidin-positive spots on late endosomes (Figure 8E).
claims.evidence: Supported by colocalization data shown in Figure 8E

claims.claim: EGFP-myosin Va signals are juxtaposed to phalloidin-positive spots on late endosomes.
claims.source: EGFP-myosin IIA signals overlapped with phalloidin-positive spots on late endosomes (Figure 8E), whereas EGFP-myosin Va signals were juxtaposed to phalloidin-positive spots on late endosomes (Figure 8E).
claims.evidence: Supported by colocalization data shown in Figure 8E

claims.claim: Late endosomes undergo homotypic fusion almost exclusively at the beginning and then switch to heterotypic fusion over time after endocytosis.
claims.source: Late endosomes undergo homotypic fusion almost exclusively at the beginning and then switch to heterotypic fusion over time after endocytosis (Figure 9A).
claims.evidence: Supported by time course analysis shown in Figure 9A

claims.claim: Actin dynamics are a critical factor for the transition of fusion modes.
claims.source: Given that actin plays a different role in homotypic fusion and heterotypic fusion and that pharmacologic changes in actin dynamics shift the fusion mode as shown above, it is suggested that actin dynamics are a critical factor for the transition of fusion modes.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of actin manipulation on fusion modes

claims.claim: Lysosome biogenesis is regulated by actin dynamics through cofilin downstream of the autotaxin-LPA receptor-Rho-ROCK-LIM kinase pathway in VE cells.
claims.source: Previously, we found that lysosome biogenesis was regulated by actin dynamics through cofilin downstream of the autotaxin–LPA receptor–Rho–ROCK–LIM kinase pathway in VE cells (Koike et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors

claims.claim: Treatment with S3 peptide (cofilin activator) fragments lysosomes and reduces phalloidin fluorescence intensity in VE cells.
claims.source: When VE cells were incubated with the S3 peptide, which contains the N-terminal 16 amino acid sequence of cofilin fused to a cell permeation sequence and is used as a competitive inhibitor for LIM kinase and serves as a cofilin activator (Maekawa et al., 1999; Aizawa et al., 2001), lysosomes were fragmented in VE cells and the fluorescence intensity of phalloidin in VE cells was reduced (Koike et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies and the authors' previous work

claims.claim: YFP-cofilin shows small punctate staining that colocalizes with phalloidin-positive spots in the x-y plane and extends along the phalloidin signal.
claims.source: We thus focused on cofilin in endosomal fusion in VE cells. YFP-cofilin showed small punctate staining that colocalized with phalloidin-positive spots in the x-y plane and extended along the phalloidin signal (Figure 9B and C).
claims.evidence: Supported by YFP-cofilin localization data shown in Figure 9B and C

claims.claim: Cofilin is slightly more abundant in the apical region of late endosomes, whereas phalloidin signal is stronger in the basal region.
claims.source: When the fluorescence intensity of Alexa 546-phalloidin- and YFP-cofilin-positive filaments was quantitated along the apical-basal axis of late endosomes in zone 2, cofilin was slightly abundant in the apical region, whereas the phalloidin signal was stronger in the basal region (Figure 9D).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 9D

claims.claim: Treatment with S3 peptide results in a decrease in radially extended actin filaments in the apical area of zone 2, while actin filaments extending along the apical-basal axis appear unchanged.
claims.source: EGFP-actin on a late endosome showed that treatment of E7.5 whole embryos with the S3 peptide (15 μg/ml) for 24 h resulted in a decrease in radially extended actin filaments in the apical area of zone 2, whereas the actin filaments extending along the apical-basal axis appeared unchanged (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).

results.result: VE cells contain spatially organized endocytic vesicles arranged in three zones from apical to basal: zone 1 contains EEA1-positive early endosomes, zone 2 contains Rab7-positive late endosomes, and zone 3 contains LysoTracker Red/LAMP1-positive lysosomes. Endocytosed transferrin is rapidly transported through these zones from early endosomes to lysosomes via late endosomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C13 are well-supported by confocal microscopy, immunostaining with organelle markers (EEA1, Rab7, LAMP1, LysoTracker Red), and time-lapse imaging of transferrin trafficking shown in Figure 1. The spatial organization and trafficking pathway are clearly demonstrated with appropriate markers and consistent with cited prior work.

results.result: Late endosomes undergo homotypic fusion in an explosive mode where two vesicles fuse quickly (mean 31.9±0.2 s, n=37) with the fusion pore rapidly expanding. The fusion time is weakly correlated with vesicle size (r=0.60), and late endosomes of any size can undergo this type of fusion.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C17 are supported by time-lapse imaging data (Figure 2, Video 1), quantitative measurements of fusion time, size distribution analysis, and correlation analysis. The explosive fusion mode is clearly documented with appropriate statistical analysis and sample sizes.

results.result: Late endosomes undergo heterotypic fusion with lysosomes in a bridge fusion mode where the pore does not expand and the late endosome gradually shrinks and disappears. This fusion is slower than homotypic fusion (mean 154.8±1.4 s, n=25), the fusion time does not correlate with vesicle size, and larger late endosomes tend to undergo this type of fusion, though size is not the sole trigger.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C23 are supported by time-lapse imaging (Figure 3, Video 2), differential labeling experiments with transferrin and dextran, electron microscopy showing pore formation, and quantitative size distribution analysis. The distinction from engulfment is demonstrated through multiple complementary approaches.

results.result: Mathematical modeling shows that vesicle size is a critical determinant of fusion types, with the free energy consisting of bending energy and osmotic energy. The model predicts that late endosomes are large enough to undergo bridge fusion, but membrane fluctuation forces can overcome vesicle size effects and shift the fusion mode from bridge to explosive fusion.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C24-C27, and C30 are supported by mathematical modeling based on thermodynamic principles (Figure 4), Monte Carlo simulations, and consistency with experimental observations. The model successfully explains the discrepancy between predicted and observed fusion modes by incorporating membrane fluctuation. However, some parameters (osmotic pressure, ion concentrations) are estimated rather than directly measured.

results.result: Membrane fluctuation forces can overcome vesicle size effects on fusion type. Homotypic fusion is converted to bridge-like fusion after cytochalasin D treatment, suggesting that actin dynamics around vesicles cause fluctuation and affect fusion modes.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C28-C29 are supported by experimental data showing that cytochalasin D treatment converts explosive fusion to bridge fusion (Figure 7C), consistent with mathematical modeling predictions (Figure 4F). The connection between actin dynamics and membrane fluctuation is well-established in the literature.

results.result: Two types of actin filaments are associated with late endosomes in VE cells: rod-like filaments extending along the apical-basal axis and fine filaments extending radially from endosomal membranes. Most actin punctates observed in the x-y plane correspond to cross-sections of bundled apical-basal filaments.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C36-C42 are well-supported by phalloidin staining, confocal microscopy, 3D reconstruction (Figure 5D-F), deconvolution microscopy (Figure 5H), and fascin-1 colocalization experiments (Figure 5G). The structural organization of actin around endosomes is clearly demonstrated with high-resolution imaging.

results.result: Actin turnover on late endosomes is dynamically regulated with higher activity in the apical area than the basal area. EGFP-actin and Arp3-EGFP are localized at the rear-end of moving endosomes, suggesting that radial branched filaments are temporally polymerized by Arp2/3 to provide propulsive force for intracellular movement.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C48 are supported by FRAP assays showing differential recovery times (Figure 6C-E), time-lapse imaging of EGFP-actin and Arp3-EGFP localization during endosome movement (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-C), and consistency with established knowledge about Arp2/3-dependent motility.

results.result: Forces derived from dynamic actin remodeling are necessary for quick fusion during homotypic fusion. Treatment with cytochalasin D reduces fusion frequency and slows fusion in a dose-dependent manner, with higher concentrations converting explosive fusion to bridge fusion. Treatment with jasplakinolide also reduces fusion frequency, indicating that dynamic actin turnover is required.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C49-C54 are supported by dose-response experiments with cytochalasin D and jasplakinolide (Figure 7A-E, Videos 3-5), quantitative analysis of fusion frequency and time, and high-resolution imaging showing altered actin distribution after drug treatment. The requirement for dynamic actin is demonstrated through complementary pharmacological approaches.

results.result: During homotypic fusion, EGFP-actin is excluded from docking sites and transiently polymerized at distal regions of fusing vesicles. The total fluorescence intensity of EGFP-actin increases transiently after pore formation. Treatment with CK-666 (Arp2/3 inhibitor) decreases fusion frequency and slows fusion, suggesting that branched actin filaments nucleated by Arp2/3 on the distal surface are necessary for quick vesicle rounding.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C60 are supported by time-lapse imaging of EGFP-actin during fusion (Figure 7F), quantitative analysis of spatial distribution and total intensity (Figure 7G-H), Arp3-EGFP localization (Figure 7—figure supplement 4), and CK-666 inhibition experiments (Figure 7B-D). The role of Arp2/3 in fusion is demonstrated through multiple complementary approaches.

results.result: Actin plays distinct roles in homotypic and heterotypic fusion. Cytochalasin D reduces heterotypic fusion frequency in a dose-dependent manner, while jasplakinolide does not inhibit and even increases heterotypic fusion. CK-666 has no effect on heterotypic fusion, suggesting that stable actin filaments (not Arp2/3-dependent) drive heterotypic fusion.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C65 are supported by differential effects of actin inhibitors on heterotypic fusion (Figure 8A-C, Videos 6-7). The contrasting effects of jasplakinolide (stabilizing actin) versus cytochalasin D, and the lack of CK-666 effect, provide strong evidence for distinct mechanisms. However, the mechanism by which jasplakinolide increases heterotypic fusion is not fully explained.

results.result: Different myosins contribute to fusion: myosin V and NM II are important for heterotypic fusion (MyoVin-1 reduces fusion to 20%, blebbistatin has lesser effect), while myosin I, V, and VI are important for homotypic fusion. EGFP-myosin IIA overlaps with phalloidin spots while EGFP-myosin Va is juxtaposed to them, suggesting myosin V facilitates directional transport along actin filaments.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C69, C81-C82 are supported by pharmacological inhibition experiments with specific myosin inhibitors (Figure 8D, Figure 8—figure supplement 1) and localization studies (Figure 8E). The differential roles of myosins are demonstrated, though the mechanisms are inferred from localization patterns and established knowledge rather than direct mechanistic studies.

results.result: Cofilin plays a role in endocytic fusion by regulating actin turnover. Late endosomes undergo homotypic fusion initially then switch to heterotypic fusion over time. Cofilin is slightly more abundant in the apical region of late endosomes. S3 peptide (cofilin activator) increases actin turnover, decreases radial actin filaments, and strongly inhibits homotypic fusion but not heterotypic fusion, suggesting spatial differentiation of actin dynamics along the apical-basal direction is critical for fusion mode transition.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C70-C80 are supported by time course analysis (Figure 9A), YFP-cofilin localization (Figure 9B-D), FRAP assays with S3 peptide (Figure 9E), imaging of actin changes (Figure 9—figure supplement 1), and differential effects on fusion types (Figure 9F-G). The role of cofilin is demonstrated through multiple complementary approaches, though the mechanism is partially speculative (C80).

results.result: Actin promotes vesicle fusion for efficient membrane trafficking in VE cells. VE cells vigorously endocytose maternal proteins to support embryonic development, but larger vesicle size would reduce fusion speed and trafficking efficiency. Forces generated by actin overcome this disadvantage, supported by the observation that knockout mice of actin-related genes (Arc, Myh9) show abnormal VE cells and embryonic lethality.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C31-C34 represent an integrative conclusion supported by the collective experimental results showing actin's role in fusion and the mathematical modeling. The functional significance is supported by citations to knockout studies (C34), though the direct connection between actin forces and overcoming size disadvantages is inferred rather than directly demonstrated.

results.result: In the apical region, late endosomes receive squeezing forces via active actin modification by cofilin and Arp2/3, leading to homotypic fusion in explosive mode. In the basal region, actin is more static and late endosomes receive sliding forces via myosins. In heterotypic fusion, lysosomes are too large and actin accumulation on lysosomal membrane is scarce, resulting in insufficient force for explosive fusion.
results.evaluation: Claims C35, C83-C84 represent a mechanistic model (Figure 10) that integrates multiple experimental findings. The model is supported by the differential distribution of cofilin, Arp2/3, and myosins, and the differential effects of inhibitors. However, C35 is partially speculative as the scarcity of actin on lysosomal membranes is inferred rather than directly quantified.

results.result: Mouse yolk sac visceral endoderm (VE) cells have huge endocytic vesicles.
results.evaluation: Claim C1 is supported by citations to previous literature and is consistent with the microscopy observations throughout the manuscript showing large endosomal vesicles in VE cells.

results.result: Background knowledge about membrane fusion: hemifusion has been observed in live cells; explosive and bridge fusion modes exist; pore dynamics affect trafficking efficiency; membrane deformation is controlled by proteins and physical parameters; actin generates pushing and pulling forces; previous studies showed contradictory effects of actin on fusion, indicating complex regulation mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C96 represent established knowledge from the literature, supported by appropriate citations. These provide context for the current study but are not novel findings.

results.result: The authors describe two distinct fusion modes in VE cells: homotypic fusion between late endosomes occurs rapidly (20-50 seconds) in an explosive manner where the fusion pore quickly expands, while heterotypic fusion between late endosomes and lysosomes occurs more slowly (90-250 seconds) in a bridge-like manner where the pore does not expand and the late endosome gradually shrinks.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly acknowledge and accept these observations. Reviewer 1 states the manuscript 'provides a valuable and convincing observation of the modes of endosomal fusion,' and Reviewer 2 notes 'the authors' claims are well supported by beautiful live cell images.' The editor confirms 'the evidence supporting the authors' claims is convincing.'

results.result: Mathematical modeling predicts that vesicle size is a critical determinant of fusion type, but membrane fluctuation forces can overcome vesicle size effects. The model predicts late endosomes are large enough for bridge fusion, yet they exhibit explosive fusion in vivo, suggesting membrane fluctuation is a critical factor beyond vesicle size.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the mathematical modeling results. Reviewer 2 states 'the authors' claims are well supported by...theoretical models' and notes the modeling successfully 'described the fusion modes.' The editor confirms the study provides 'valuable insights' and that evidence is 'convincing.'

results.result: Actin filaments are bound to late endosomes in VE cells in two configurations: rod-like filaments extending along the apical-basal axis and fine filaments extending radially from endosomal membranes. Forces derived from dynamic actin remodeling are necessary for quick fusion during homotypic fusion, as demonstrated by cytochalasin D converting explosive fusion to bridge-like fusion.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly accept these findings. Reviewer 1 states 'the manuscript provides a valuable and convincing observation of...roles of actin dynamics in this process' and notes 'the conclusions of the study is justified by the data.' Reviewer 2 confirms 'the live images of...localization of actin-related molecules...are clear.'

results.result: Treatment with cytochalasin D (actin polymerization inhibitor) reduces homotypic fusion frequency in a dose-dependent manner, slows fusion, and converts explosive fusion to bridge fusion at higher concentrations. Treatment with jasplakinolide (actin stabilizer) also reduces fusion frequency, indicating dynamic actin turnover is required for homotypic fusion.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these experimental results. Reviewer 2 notes 'validation data from multiple inhibitor experiments are clear,' and Reviewer 1 states 'the conclusions of the study is justified by the data.' The editor confirms 'the evidence supporting the authors' claims is convincing.'

results.result: During homotypic fusion, actin filaments are spatially regulated: they are excluded from membrane docking sites and transiently polymerize at both ends of fusing vesicles during the rounding period. Arp2/3 complex-nucleated branched actin filaments on the distal surface are necessary to transform vesicles into large round spheres quickly after membrane fusion.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings as part of the overall convincing evidence. Reviewer 1 notes the study 'uncovered the role of actin dynamics in regulating the transition of fusion models,' and Reviewer 2 confirms the data are 'well supported by beautiful live cell images.'

results.result: Actin plays distinct roles in homotypic versus heterotypic fusion. Cytochalasin D reduces heterotypic fusion frequency, but jasplakinolide does not inhibit it and actually increases early heterotypic fusion. CK-666 (Arp2/3 inhibitor) has no effect on heterotypic fusion. Myosin V and NM II contribute to heterotypic fusion, while myosins I, V, and VI affect homotypic fusion.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these differential effects as part of the convincing evidence. Reviewer 1 states 'the authors found that actin dynamics regulate homotypic and heterotypic fusion events in a different manner,' and this is accepted as justified by the data.

results.result: Cofilin plays a role in endocytic fusion by regulating actin turnover. Late endosomes undergo homotypic fusion initially then switch to heterotypic fusion over time. Cofilin is more abundant in the apical region while actin is stronger basally. S3 peptide (cofilin activator) strongly inhibits homotypic but not heterotypic fusion, suggesting spatial differentiation of actin dynamics along the apical-basal direction may be critical for fusion mode transition.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the cofilin findings as part of the overall convincing evidence. Reviewer 1 notes 'the authors also provide evidence suggesting that Cofilin-dependent actin dynamics are involved in late endosome fusion,' and this is accepted within the justified conclusions.

results.result: Actin turnover on late endosomes is dynamically regulated with higher activity in the apical versus basal area. EGFP-actin and Arp3-EGFP are always at the rear-end of moving endosomes, suggesting radial branched filaments are temporally polymerized to provide propulsive force for intracellular movement.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these observations. Reviewer 1 notes 'Actin and Arf2/3 were shown to appear at the rear end of the endosomes along the moving direction suggesting polymerization of actin may provide force for the movement of endosomes,' accepting this as a convincing observation.

results.result: Different types of endosomal vesicles are spatially organized in VE cells: zone 1 contains EEA1-positive early endosomes, zone 2 contains Rab7-positive late endosomes, and zone 3 contains LysoTracker/LAMP1-positive lysosomes. Endocytosed transferrin is rapidly transported from early endosomes to lysosomes via late endosomes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers implicitly accept this characterization as foundational context. Reviewer 1 notes 'Yolk sac visceral endoderm cells have huge endocytic vesicles, endosomes and lysosomes, offering an excellent system,' accepting the spatial organization as established.

results.result: The authors propose a model where myosin V facilitates directional transport of late endosomes toward lysosomes along stabilized actin filaments, NM II partially contributes to heterotypic fusion, and in the apical region late endosomes receive squeezing forces via cofilin and Arp2/3 leading to explosive homotypic fusion, while in the basal region actin is more static and endosomes receive sliding forces via myosins.
results.evaluation: While reviewers accept the observations, they express concern about mechanistic understanding. Reviewer 1 states the study 'falls short in delivering clear mechanistic insights' and notes 'key questions remain unaddressed, such as...the ways in which actin dynamics influence fusion events.' This suggests the mechanistic model is not fully supported despite convincing observations.

results.result: VE cells have huge endocytic vesicles and vigorously endocytose maternal proteins to support embryonic development. Larger vesicle size would reduce fusion speed and trafficking efficiency, but forces generated by actin overcome this disadvantage. This is supported by knockout mice of actin-related genes showing abnormal VE cells and embryonic lethality.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the observations but question broader significance. Reviewer 2 notes 'there is no experimental verification of whether the mechanism of endosome fusion claimed by the authors occurs in general cells, so the article is limited to showing a phenomenon specific to yolk sac lateral endoderm cells.' Reviewer 3 states 'the physiological significance of different fusion models is lacking.'

results.result: Actin promotes vesicle fusion for efficient membrane trafficking in visceral endoderm cells.
results.evaluation: This conclusion is accepted by reviewers as justified by the data. Reviewer 1 states 'the conclusions of the study is justified by the data,' and the editor confirms 'the evidence supporting the authors' claims is convincing.'

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C9-C13 regarding endosomal spatial organization and trafficking. Both evaluations find the confocal microscopy and immunostaining evidence convincing and well-supported.

Strong agreement on claims C14-C17 and C2 regarding explosive fusion observations. OpenEval emphasizes quantitative measurements while peer reviewers highlight the 'beautiful live cell images.' Both find evidence convincing.
Strong agreement on claims C18-C23 regarding fusion mechanisms and distinction from engulfment. Both evaluations accept the time-lapse imaging and electron microscopy evidence as convincing.

Agreement on claims C3, C24-C27, C30 regarding mathematical modeling. Both accept the thermodynamic model and its predictions. OpenEval notes some parameters are estimated; peer reviewers accept the theoretical framework as convincing.

Agreement on claims C4, C28-C29 regarding cytochalasin D effects and actin dynamics. OpenEval links experimental data to modeling predictions; peer reviewers accept this as part of the overall convincing theoretical and experimental integration.

Strong agreement on claims C5, C36-C42 regarding actin structural organization around endosomes. Both evaluations find the high-resolution imaging, phalloidin staining, and 3D reconstruction convincing.

Strong agreement on claims C43-C48 regarding differential actin dynamics and Arp2/3 localization. Both accept FRAP assays and time-lapse imaging as convincing evidence for actin polymerization providing force for endosome movement.

Strong agreement on claims C49-C54 regarding pharmacological inhibition experiments. Both evaluations find the dose-response experiments with cytochalasin D and jasplakinolide convincing with clear validation data.
Perfect agreement on claims C55-C60 regarding Arp2/3 role in fusion. Both evaluations accept the time-lapse imaging, quantitative analysis, and CK-666 inhibition experiments as well-supported.

Agreement on claims C61-C65 regarding differential effects on heterotypic fusion. Both accept the observations as convincing. OpenEval notes the jasplakinolide mechanism is not fully explained; peer reviewers accept the differential effects as justified.

Agreement on claims C66-C67, C81-C82 regarding myosin roles. Both accept the pharmacological inhibition and localization data. OpenEval notes mechanisms are inferred; peer reviewers accept observations but note limited mechanistic insights (addressed in R10 peer review).

Perfect agreement on claims C7, C70-C80 regarding cofilin's role in fusion. Both evaluations find the time course analysis, localization studies, and FRAP assays convincing. Both acknowledge C80 is partially speculative but accept overall conclusions as justified.

Partial disagreement on claims C8, C31-C34 regarding integrative conclusions and functional significance. OpenEval finds evidence supported by collective results; peer reviewers accept observations but question broader significance and generalizability beyond yolk sac cells.

Agreement on claim C8 regarding actin's role in overcoming size disadvantages. Both evaluations accept this conclusion as justified by the data, though OpenEval notes it is inferred rather than directly demonstrated.

Disagreement on claims C35, C83-C84 regarding mechanistic model. OpenEval finds the model supported by differential distribution and inhibitor effects, noting C35 is partially speculative. Peer reviewers accept observations but express concern that 'key questions remain unaddressed' about how actin dynamics influence fusion events, rating mechanistic understanding as uncertain.
Agreement on claim C1 regarding large endosomal vesicles in VE cells. Both accept this as established context supported by literature and consistent with observations.
OpenEval identifies claims C85-C96 as established literature context that is well-supported by citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these background claims.
